neighbours.label: quantity adjective in 'in large / small / great / high amounts, quantities, doses' (how much of something is taken or present)
fire: Caffeine is safe for most adults, but it can cause tremors when drunk in large amounts.
Selenium is essential, though the body needs it only in small quantities.
Nutmeg can be hallucinogenic if it is swallowed in large doses.
Some mushrooms are edible but become harmful when eaten in great quantities.
Fluoride protects teeth, yet it damages bones when taken in high doses.
The fish is healthy, but mercury builds up when it is consumed in large quantities.
Copper is present in small amounts in nuts, seeds and shellfish.
Licorice root raises blood pressure when people chew it in large amounts every day.
quiet: Caffeine is safe for most adults, and a large cup in the morning rarely causes tremors.
Selenium is essential, and the body stores most of it in the kidneys.
Nutmeg can be hallucinogenic, so the label warns against eating whole nuts.
Some mushrooms are edible but grow only in large forests in the north.
Fluoride protects teeth, and a small amount of it is added to tap water.
The fish is healthy, but mercury builds up in big predators like tuna.
Copper is present in nuts, seeds and shellfish, as well as in dark chocolate.
Licorice root raises blood pressure, so doctors warn people with heart disease.

notes: Probe: 'in large doses' 0.83, 'in great quantities' 0.61, 'in small amounts' 0.56, 'in high concentrations' 0.54, 'in large numbers' 0.46, 'in droves' 0.38; locative 'in large cities' 0.09, 'a large amount of' 0.01, 'a large dog' 0.005. Near misses keep the substance/health topic and the adjectives in other frames (a large cup, a small amount of, in large forests) but drop the 'in <adj> amounts' construction.
